name: TCAN1043ADRQ1
title: TCAN1043A-Q1 / TCAN1043AT-Q1: automotive CAN FD transceiver with sleep mode, INH output and local wake input
summary: A high-speed CAN and CAN FD transceiver for vehicles, AEC-Q100 qualified, meeting the ISO 11898-2:2016 physical layer. It runs from three supplies: VSUP from the battery (4.5 V to 40 V), VCC at 5 V for the bus driver, and VIO from 1.7 V to 5.5 V for the logic pins. A high-voltage INH output switches the node's regulators off in sleep, when only the transceiver stays alive (18 µA typ from VSUP) and watches the bus for a wake-up pattern and the WAKE pin for an edge. The bus pins survive ±58 V; TCAN1043A-Q1 handles data rates to 8 Mbps and TCAN1043AT-Q1 to 5 Mbps, in 14-pin SOIC, SOT-23-THIN and VSON packages.
key_figures: 4.5 V to 40 V; 45 V load dump for 300 ms
140 ns typ, 215 ns max recessive to dominant (TCAN1043A-Q1)
±8 kV HBM on bus, VSUP and WAKE; ±15 kV air (SAE J2962-2)

notes: TCAN1043A-Q1 (8 Mbps) comes in SOIC, SOT-23-THIN and VSON; TCAN1043AT-Q1 (5 Mbps) comes in SOIC and VSON. The data rate of each family is given on page 1; the two differ in loop delay, driver propagation delay and bit-time limits.
The VSON marking is two lines: TCAN over 1043A, or TCAN over 043AT.

pins.name: TXD
pins.function: Transmit data from the CAN controller, referred to VIO; low drives the bus dominant. An internal pull-up to VIO holds it recessive when left open.

pins.name: GND
pins.function: Ground; tie to the board ground.

pins.name: VCC
pins.function: 5 V supply of the CAN driver and receiver.

pins.name: RXD
pins.function: Received data to the CAN controller, referred to VIO; low for a dominant bus. Goes low to flag a wake-up in standby. High impedance while VIO is below its undervoltage level.

pins.name: VIO
pins.function: Logic-level supply, 1.7 V to 5.5 V, setting the levels of TXD, RXD, EN, nSTB and nFAULT.

pins.name: EN
pins.function: Mode select, used together with nSTB; internal pull-down.

pins.name: INH
pins.function: Inhibit output, near VSUP in every mode but sleep and high impedance in sleep; drives the enable input of the node's regulators.

pins.name: nFAULT
pins.function: Active-low status output carrying the fault, power-up and wake-source flags; high impedance in sleep.

pins.name: WAKE
pins.function: Local wake-up input; either a rising or a falling edge wakes the device from sleep.

pins.name: VSUP
pins.function: Battery supply, feeding the internal regulators for the digital core and the low-power wake receiver.

pins.name: nSTB
pins.function: Standby control, used together with EN for mode selection; internal pull-down.

pins.name: Thermal Pad
pins.function: VSON (DMT) only: exposed pad, soldered to the board ground plane for heat sinking.

circuits.title: Typical application
circuits.description: One CAN FD node powered from the battery. VBAT passes a series diode; the protected rail feeds a regulator's input, the transceiver's VSUP (100 nF to ground) and a wake switch network. The regulator gives 5 V to VCC and a separate rail to VIO and the microcontroller's VDD, each with 100 nF at the transceiver pin. INH drives the regulator's enable with 100 kΩ to ground, so sleep turns the node's power off. From the protected rail 3 kΩ pulls up a node that a push switch shorts to ground; that node carries 22 nF to ground and reaches WAKE through 33 kΩ. Three microcontroller GPIOs drive EN and nSTB and read nFAULT; its CAN FD controller drives TXD and reads RXD. CANH and CANL go to the bus.

parts.note: regulator with enable, 5 V output and a VIO output
on the protected rail at the regulator input
wake node pull-up from the protected rail

notes: An optional terminating node (split termination) and optional filtering, transient and ESD parts can sit across CANH and CANL on the bus side; no values are given for them.
VCC and VIO can also share one 5 V regulator.

circuits.title: WAKE input with a high-side switch
circuits.description: A switch from VSUP pulls a node high against RBIAS to ground; the node reaches WAKE through RSERIES. RSERIES limits the WAKE current during a ground shift or ground loss, and RBIAS holds the node low with the switch open.

parts.note: 15 kΩ minimum for a 45 V supply and 3 mA; below 50 kΩ preferred
below 330 kΩ for a 45 V supply

notes: The other pins of U1 are not part of this circuit.

circuits.title: WAKE input with a low-side switch
circuits.description: RBIAS from VSUP holds a node high and a switch to ground pulls it low; the node reaches WAKE through RSERIES, which limits the WAKE current during a ground shift or ground loss.

parts.note: 15 kΩ minimum for a 45 V supply and 3 mA; below 50 kΩ preferred

circuits.title: Standard bus termination
circuits.description: A single resistor RTERM across CANH and CANL; one is fitted at both bus ends, in the cable or inside a node that terminates.

circuits.title: Split bus termination
circuits.description: RTERM divided into two equal halves in series across CANH and CANL, with CSPLIT from their junction to ground. The capacitor filters common-mode noise and steadies the bus common-mode voltage, improving emissions.
notes: The 60 Ω halves and the 1 nF to 100 nF capacitor come from the layout guidelines (page 41).

circuits.title: Protected node of the layout example
circuits.description: The full node behind the example layout. 0.1 µF bypasses VCC and VIO, and VSUP carries 0.1 µF and 15 µF. INH has 100 kΩ to ground. WAKE goes through 33 kΩ to a switch input that carries 3 kΩ to VSUP and 22 nF to ground. nSTB has a resistor to the microcontroller supply. The bus lines pass a common-mode choke, then a split termination of two 60 Ω resistors with a capacitor from the centre to ground, a 0.1 µF filter capacitor from each line to ground, and a TVS at the connector J1.

parts.note: bidirectional TVS diode or varistor rated for the application; pins 1 and 3 on the lines, 2 to ground

notes: Choke pins 1-2 carry CANH and 3-4 carry CANL.

circuits.title: Test circuit
circuits.description: General bus load for the electrical tables: two RL/2 halves in series across CANH and CANL with CL1 from their centre to ground, CL2 across the lines, and CL(RXD) from RXD to ground. TXD and nSTB are driven.
notes: The supplies and other pins of U1 are not part of this circuit.

circuits.title: Supply test circuit
circuits.description: RL and CL in parallel across CANH and CANL with TXD driven, for the supply-current rows.
notes: The supplies and other pins of U1 are not part of this circuit.

circuits.title: Driver test circuit
circuits.description: RL and CL in parallel across the bus, plus an RCM resistor from each line to a common-mode source VCM. VOD is read across the lines and VO(CANH), VO(CANL) from each line to ground; tpLD, tpHR, tR and tF are taken from TXD's 50% points and VOD's 0.9 V, 0.5 V, 10% and 90% points.
notes: The supplies and other pins of U1 are not part of this circuit.

circuits.title: Receiver test circuit
circuits.description: VID applied between CANH and CANL; RXD loads CL_RXD to ground. tpRH and tpDL run from VID crossing 0.5 V and 0.9 V (between 0 V and 1.5 V) to RXD's 50% point; tR and tF are RXD's 10% to 90% times.
notes: The supplies and other pins of U1 are not part of this circuit.

circuits.title: Transmitter and receiver timing test circuit
circuits.description: TXD driven with VI; RL and CL across the bus; RXD loads CL_RXD. The loop delays run from TXD's 30% and 70% points to RXD's; after five long bits a short bit tBIT(TXD) is sent, and tBIT(BUS) is measured on VDIFF at 900 mV and 500 mV, tBIT(RXD) at RXD's 30% and 70% points.

operation.text: A CAN FD transceiver to ISO 11898-2:2016 with three supplies (VSUP, VCC, VIO). VIO lets it talk to 1.8 V, 2.5 V, 3.3 V or 5 V controllers directly. Its INH output gates the node's regulators so that only the transceiver draws battery current in sleep, and a bus wake-up pattern or a WAKE edge brings INH back high to start the node. Protection covers undervoltage on every supply, bus-fault detection, the SWE timer, battery connection detection, thermal shutdown, TXD dominant timeout and ±58 V on the bus.

VSUP comes from the battery and powers the internal regulators for the digital core and the low-power bus receiver. VCC is the 5 V supply of the CAN driver and receiver. VIO, 1.7 V to 5.5 V, sets the logic levels to match the controller.

TXD, RXD, nFAULT, EN and nSTB all work at VIO levels. TXD is pulled to VIO so an open pin reads recessive. RXD drives to VIO once VIO is valid and is pulled low on a power-on or wake-up event. nFAULT carries the status flags and goes high impedance in sleep, where no fault is reported. EN and nSTB together choose the mode; both have internal pull-downs that keep a floating pin from raising power or causing a false wake-up.

INH is a high-voltage output that stays on in every mode except sleep, where it goes high impedance. It is a logic signal for the enable pin of a regulator, not a power switch, and it has no reverse-battery protection, so it stays inside the module. A 100 kΩ load to ground speeds its fall from high to low and holds it low when it floats.

WAKE is a high-voltage, reverse-blocked local wake-up input. It reacts to both rising and falling edges, so a switch to VSUP or to ground both work. An unused WAKE is tied to VSUP or ground to stop stray wake-ups. The local wake circuit runs in sleep and is off in normal mode. A level change counts only if it stays past tWAKE_HT.

nFAULT reports faults ORed together, plus wake requests and a cold start on VSUP so the controller can run cold-boot or diagnostic code. RXD reports a wake-up request. PWRON is set whenever VSUP rises above UVSUP(R) after an undervoltage or a new battery connection, shows as nFAULT low on entering silent mode from standby or sleep, and clears on entering normal mode. Entering silent mode first and reading nFAULT tells a cold start (low) from a wake-up (high); after that, WAKESR in normal mode tells a local wake (low) from a remote one (high).

In the three low-power modes (standby, go-to-sleep and sleep), a valid local or remote wake-up, or power-up on VSUP, sets WAKERQ. Setting it resets the tUV timers. It clears on entering normal mode or during a VCC or VIO undervoltage.

Every supply has an undervoltage detector; these flags are internal and never reach nFAULT. UVSUP sets when VSUP falls below its threshold, and PWRON and WAKERQ set once it recovers. UVCC and UVIO set only after the supply stays low for longer than tUV. A VSUP undervoltage turns the CAN transceiver off. A VCC undervoltage leaves the device in normal or silent mode with the transceiver in autonomous active and RXD high while VIO is present; past tUV the device goes to sleep. A VIO undervoltage sends it to standby, and to sleep past tUV. In all cases the bus pins present no load. After the supplies recover it takes typically 200 µs to return to normal operation.

While driving dominant the device watches for six shorts: CANH or CANL to VBAT, VCC or GND. A fault that persists for four dominant-to-recessive transitions pulls nFAULT low in normal mode; the driver keeps running so the node can still communicate until the system decides. Four fault-free transitions clear the flag. Detection works for differential loads within RCBF and faults lasting longer than tCBF. Full coverage needs a diagnostic step in each node reported to a central point.

If TXD is low before CAN active mode is entered, the driver stays off and the bus recessive; the receiver keeps working. nFAULT shows it on entering silent mode from normal mode. Power-up clears it, as does reaching CAN active with TXD already high, or TXD high at a moment RXD is low, provided no other local fault is present.

A falling edge on TXD starts a timer; if TXD has not risen within tTXDDTO the driver releases the bus to recessive so a stuck node cannot block the network. The receiver keeps mirroring the bus. The driver returns on the next dominant-to-recessive edge on TXD. The timeout limits the lowest data rate (see the minimum data rate equation).

operation.topic: TXD shorted to RXD and bus stuck dominant
operation.text: TXDRXD sets when TXD and RXD are shorted for tTXDDTO or more; the driver stays off until it clears. CANDOM sets when the bus stays dominant longer than tBUSDOM; the driver stays enabled. Both show on nFAULT on entering silent mode from normal mode and clear on the next suitable edge or on any change to normal, standby, go-to-sleep or sleep mode.
TXDCLP, TXDDTO, TXDRXD, CANDOM and TSD are detected in normal and silent modes but reported on nFAULT only on the move from normal to silent mode; any other mode change clears them.

Above TSDR the driver turns off, the bus goes to the recessive bias and the receiver path stays working. The fault clears below TSDF; hysteresis keeps the driver from oscillating. If the cause remains, the cycle repeats, and prolonged operation in thermal shutdown can hurt reliability. The event is reported on nFAULT.
With no supply the bus pins and logic pins leak very little, so an unpowered node loads neither the bus nor the circuits round it.
The internal pull-ups and pull-downs are a fail-safe, not a design feature to rely on. An open-drain controller output on TXD needs an external pull-up strong enough to keep CAN FD bit timing.

Driver current limiting in both states and the TXD dominant timeout cap the current into a shorted line. Because the bus alternates, and CAN forces recessive time through bit stuffing, control fields and interframe space, the average short-circuit current (equation above) is what sizes termination resistors and the common-mode choke.

Six modes: normal, silent, standby, go-to-sleep, sleep and off (protected), chosen by EN and nSTB together with the supplies, temperature and wake events. EN high, nSTB high: normal. EN low, nSTB high: silent. EN low, nSTB low: standby. EN high, nSTB low: go-to-sleep, then sleep after tGOTOSLEEP once WAKERQ is clear. VSUP below UVSUP(F) puts the device in power off with bus, INH and RXD high impedance. VCC or VIO staying below its threshold for longer than tUV sends it to sleep from any mode.

Normal mode drives TXD onto the bus and reports the bus on RXD; entering it clears WAKERQ and PWRON and stops and resets the SWE timer. Silent mode is listen-only: driver off, receiver on, and nFAULT shows PWRON and local faults. Silent entered from standby keeps the SWE timer running; if it expires the device goes to sleep.

Standby turns off driver and receiver but keeps INH on so the system can run. RXD low marks a wake-up request; the source is read on nFAULT after the move to normal mode. The SWE timer starts on entering standby; if the controller has not put the device in normal mode within tINACTIVE (about 4 min), the device drops to sleep. At power-up the tUV timers stay off, giving VCC and VIO up to tINACTIVE to come up; each timer arms once its supply passes its rising threshold.

The passing state on the way to sleep: driver and receiver off, INH still on. After tGOTOSLEEP the device sleeps and INH goes high impedance. A pending wake-up event keeps the device in standby until normal mode clears it.

The lowest-power mode. Driver and main receiver are off; the low-power receiver watches the bus for a wake-up pattern and the WAKE circuit watches for an edge, and INH is off so the node's regulators shut down. Sleep ends on a valid wake-up pattern, a WAKE event, or a rising edge on nSTB. EN may be either level in sleep; low or floating gives the least current. When sleep followed go-to-sleep or a supply undervoltage on VCC or VIO, nSTB rising takes the device out: EN high at that edge selects normal, EN low selects silent. VIO has to be above UVIO(R).

operation.topic: Leaving sleep after an SWE timeout
operation.text: When sleep followed an SWE timeout, going straight to normal needs nSTB high and a rising edge on EN; to silent, nSTB high and a falling edge on EN. If nSTB was already high when sleep began, EN has to toggle while nSTB is low first, and nSTB stays low at least tMODE1 after that EN edge before it is raised. VIO has to be above UVIO(R).

In standby and sleep the low-power receiver looks for the ISO 11898-2:2016 multiple-filtered wake-up pattern: a dominant, a recessive and a second dominant, each lasting at least tWK(FILTER). Other bus traffic between the phases does not reset the search. On the second dominant RXD goes low, at once if VIO is valid or as soon as VIO rises above UVIO(R). A bus state shorter than the minimum tWK(FILTER) never counts, longer than the maximum always counts, and between may count. The filter sits inside both the short and long ISO filter ranges, so one bit at 500 kbps or two at 1 Mbps meet it. The whole pattern has to arrive within tWK(TIMEOUT) or the search restarts; if the bus is dominant when the timeout ends, a recessive of at least tWK(FILTER) separates the next attempt. INH rises within tINH_SLP_STB after detection and the device goes to standby.

The bus side has four states, following the ISO 11898-2:2016 autonomous biasing scheme, which lowers RF emissions. CAN off (VSUP below UVSUP(F)): transmitter and receiver off, bus pins floating, no load on the bus and no reverse current if battery or ground is lost. CAN autonomous inactive: bus pins biased to ground through the receiver's input resistors, in standby, go-to-sleep or sleep after the bus has been quiet for tSILENCE. CAN autonomous active: bus biased to 2.5 V from VSUP after a remote wake-up, or on leaving normal or silent with the bus active within tSILENCE, or during a VCC or VIO undervoltage; it falls back to inactive after tSILENCE. CAN active: normal or silent mode with VCC and VIO valid, bus biased at VCC/2. A TXD held low before leaving standby blocks the transmitter on entering CAN active.

Dominant is a differential drive of the bus and a low on TXD and RXD; recessive is the bus resting at half of VCC through the receiver input resistors and a high on TXD and RXD. A dominant overrides a recessive in arbitration, and several drivers dominant at once give a larger differential than one. In the low-power modes after tSILENCE a third state appears: both lines pulled to ground through the input resistors.

operation.topic: Bus loading, length and node count
operation.text: A typical CAN network runs to 40 m with stubs up to 0.3 m; careful design allows longer cables and stubs and more nodes. The driver gives at least 1.5 V into 50 Ω and 1.4 V into 45 Ω. With RID of at least 50 kΩ, over 100 transceivers fit on one segment in theory; margins for cabling, loading, timing, imbalance, ground offset and signal integrity lower the practical count. Standards such as ARINC825, CANopen, DeviceNet, SAEJ2284, SAEJ1939 and NMEA200 trade rate, length and loading; CANopen, for example, reaches 1 km with fewer than 64 nodes and a much lower rate.

Each end of the bus takes a 120 Ω resistor, fitted either in the cable or inside a node that terminates. Split termination (two halves with a capacitor from the centre to ground) filters high-frequency common-mode noise and steadies the common-mode voltage, improving emissions. Termination on a board is lost if that node is removed.

VSUP connects to the battery rail, VCC takes 4.5 V to 5.5 V for the transceiver, and VIO 1.7 V to 5.5 V to match the controller. One 5 V regulator can feed both VCC and VIO, or separate 5 V and 3.3 V regulators can. A 100 nF capacitor at each supply pin, as close as possible, damps switcher ripple and the impedance of the board planes.

Transients carry high frequencies, so high-frequency layout practice applies. Protection and filtering sit next to the bus connector so transients, ESD and noise stay off the board: a bidirectional TVS or varistor (D1), optional 0.1 µF bus capacitors (C6, C7), a common-mode choke in series between the device and the connector. Protection parts lie along the signal path so transient current does not detour. Supply and ground planes keep inductance low, and bypass and protection parts use at least two vias each to supply and ground. Bypass parts sit at the pins: 0.1 µF on VCC (C1) and VIO (C2), 0.1 µF and 15 µF on VSUP (C3, C4). The example shows split termination with two 60 Ω resistors (R3, R4) and 1 nF to 100 nF (C5) to ground, 100 kΩ (R1) from INH to ground, and on WAKE 33 kΩ (R5), 3 kΩ (R6) and 22 nF (C8) to ground. VIO goes to the controller's I/O supply.
